bangus.description: The fish has an elongated, slightly compressed body with an oval cross‑section. It possesses two dorsal spines and between thirteen and seventeen soft dorsal rays, as well as two anal spines and eight to ten anal soft rays, and a total of forty‑six vertebrae. Its mouth is small and lacks teeth, and a single dorsal fin sits around the middle of the body. The pectoral fins are curved like a sickle, and the caudal fin is large and deeply forked. There are no scutes on the belly, and it has four branchiostegal rays. The body coloration is olive‑green on the back, turning silvery along the sides, while the unpaired fins have dark margins.

budlis.description: The fish has a streamlined, elongated body that is rounded in cross‑section. It possesses 14‑16 dorsal spines and 14‑15 soft rays on the dorsal fin, which is split into two parts by a tiny gap no larger than the eye; the second dorsal fin is followed by seven to nine small finlets. The anal fin lacks spines and carries 14‑15 soft rays, ending in seven to eight finlets. Its pectoral fins are short with 26‑27 rays, and there are two fleshy flaps (the interpelvic process) situated between the pelvic fins. The species has a total of 41 vertebrae and 53‑63 gill rakers on the first gill arch. The teeth are small, cone‑shaped, and arranged in a single row. The body is essentially scaleless except for a bony band (corselet) and the lateral line; strong keels run along each side of the caudal‑fin base, flanked by two smaller keels. In life the back appears a dark purplish‑blue, while the lower sides and belly are silvery, marked by four to six very noticeable dark longitudinal bands that may look like a series of dark blotches.

tamban.description: This fish has no dorsal or anal spines, but it does possess a moderate number of soft rays—about 13 to 21 along the dorsal fin and 12 to 23 along the anal fin. A faint golden spot can be seen just behind the gill opening, accompanied by a subtle golden line running mid‑laterally along the body, and a distinct black spot marks the rear edge of the gill cover where pigment is absent. Its body is elongated and almost cylindrical in shape, with a compressed, fusiform profile that gives it a streamlined appearance. It can be told apart from other clupeids in the eastern Indian Ocean and western Pacific by the presence of eight pelvic fin rays, and it differs from *S. longiceps* by having a shorter head and fewer lower gill rakers.

tilapia.description: The fish is a large, deep‑bodied tilapia with a relatively small head. It has 15‑18 dorsal spines, 11‑13 soft rays on the dorsal fin, three anal spines and 9‑11 anal soft rays, and a total of 30‑32 vertebrae. Its body is fusiform and laterally compressed, with a depth that reaches roughly one‑third to one‑half of its standard length. In mature males the lower jaw is only about a third to a little more than a third of the head length, and the breeding male’s genital papilla is smooth rather than tasselled. A key identifying feature at every life stage is the presence of regular vertical stripes that run through the entire depth of the caudal (tail) fin; in younger fish these stripes are broader, form an arc, and begin at the base of the tail. Adult males are typically bluish‑pink, sometimes showing a dark throat, belly, anal, and pelvic fins, while females are usually brownish above with silvery‑white undersides and display about ten thin vertical bars.

sagision.description: The fish possesses ten dorsal spines and nine soft rays on the dorsal fin, together with three spines and seven soft rays on the anal fin. It lacks a suborbital spine, and the preopercle is marked by three transverse rows of scales. Its pectoral fins are long, extending to about the level of the anus and the origin of the anal fin, while the pelvic fins are even longer, reaching the origin of the anal fin or extending beyond it. The upper lobe of the caudal fin is slightly rounded and has a rosy hue. A distinct line runs upward from the back edge of the suborbital region to the dorsal profile, meeting the side about two to four scales before the dorsal fin begins, and an axillary scale is present. The upper part of the body is pinkish, transitioning to a silvery‑white underside, and two silvery‑mauve lines run in front of and below the eye. The fish has a fusiform, or torpedo‑shaped, body with an oval cross‑section.

burao.description: The fish has a streamlined, fusiform body with an oval cross‑section and a head that extends longer than the depth of its body. Its dorsal fin is supported by eight to eleven spines and twelve soft rays, while the anal fin lacks spines and has twelve soft rays, and the total number of vertebrae is thirty‑one. The maxilla is covered by the lachrymal bone, and a small, single interpelvic process is present. The anal spine is only rudimentary. Along the longest gill raker, there are between thirty and fifty‑five bristles, but the gill rakers do not reach far into the mouth. A distinctive black blotch sits just behind the base of the pectoral fin, and the belly shines a yellow‑silvery color. At the base of the first dorsal fin, there are two to six large spots, and some individuals display two faint stripes that run along the level of the lateral line. The fish also possesses a functional swim bladder.

talho.description: The fish has no dorsal or anal spines and about eleven to twelve soft rays on each of those fins. Its body is elongated and cigar‑shaped, with a rounded or slightly compressed profile and a circular cross‑section. The head is pointed and flattened, and the snout is rounded. The dorsal fin starts nearer the small adipose fin than to the tip of the snout, while the anal fin begins closer to the base of the tail than to the gill cover. Its coloration is brown‑gray on the top and creamy underneath, marked by several faint, darker spots running along the middle of its sides.

sapsap.description: The fish has eight dorsal spines and fifteen to sixteen soft dorsal rays, with three anal spines and fourteen to fifteen soft anal rays. Its body is unusually deep and laterally compressed, giving it a strongly humped back; the depth of the body is about one‑seventh to one‑ninth of its total length. When the mouth is opened it points downward, and the gill rakers are short, fleshy and less than half the length of the gill lamellae, with a total of eighteen to twenty‑two on the first gill arch. The head and breast are smooth and scaleless, while the lateral line is lined with tube‑like scales numbering sixty‑one to sixty‑six. Adults have a greyish back, a silvery belly, and many faint, closely spaced parallel bars on the back, often with a dark brown saddle marking on the caudal peduncle. The area around the pectoral fins is grey to black, the edge of the soft dorsal fin is black, and both lobes of the tail fin have broad, dusky margins. The pectoral, pelvic, and anal fins range from colourless to a pale yellow. Juveniles (about five to seven centimetres long) display thin, closely spaced grey vertical lines that run from the back down to about mid‑height, a noticeably yellow membrane between the anal‑fin spines, pale‑yellow and dusky edges on the tail‑fin lobes, mostly clear fins, and a snout dotted with black. The overall body shape is short and deep, with a laterally compressed cross‑section.

moonfish.description: This fish has a very deep, almost triangular body that is extremely laterally compressed, giving it a sharp‑edged breast. Its greatest depth is found below the lateral line, which is at least four times deeper than the area above the line. The anal fin is unusually long, starting at the point where the pelvic fins attach, and it runs low along the body. Juveniles have about ten dorsal spines, but the number of spines decreases as the fish ages, ending up with three to four spines and forty to forty‑five soft dorsal rays in adults; the anal fin has no spines and thirty to thirty‑three soft rays. The upper sides of the body shine a deep metallic blue while the rest is silvery, adorned with a row of round‑to‑ovoid dark slate‑blue spots that run above and below the lateral line, sometimes accompanied by a few extra spots. The pelvic fins show a faint hint of blue, and the remaining fins are mostly transparent or only slightly dusky.
